The Museum of Unfinished Things

There is a museum I sometimes visit in my mind. It has no address and no opening hours. You don't buy a ticket; you just end up there, usually around 2 a.m., or on a rainy Tuesday when you were supposed to be doing something else.

Its galleries are vast and quiet, lit with that soft, amber light that makes everything look more important than it is. And on every pedestal, behind every pane of glass, is something unfinished.

There's the half-knitted sweater, abandoned when the knitter realized she had made it three sizes too big. There's the novel with only three chapters written, the language-learning app streak that ended at 47 days, the garden that was weeded once in April and then surrendered to the weeds. There is the guitar with only the first three chords learned, slightly out of tune. There is my own contribution - several of them, actually. A stack of notebooks filled a third of the way. A folder on a hard drive named "ideas_final_FINAL_v2."

Most of us are taught to be ashamed of this wing of our lives. We are told that unfinished is the same as failed. That discipline is finishing what you start, no matter what. That quitters never win.

But I have come to love the Museum of Unfinished Things, because it tells a more honest story about what it means to be human than any hall of trophies ever could.

Finished things are impressive. They are neat. They have clear edges. You can put them on a resume or an Instagram carousel. "I ran a marathon." "I wrote a book." "I learned Japanese." They are monuments.

Unfinished things are maps. They show you where your curiosity tried to go.

That sweater that was too big? Someone cared enough to try to make something warm with their own hands. That novel with three chapters? Someone had a world inside them that wanted to get out, even if it only got three chapters out. The 47-day streak in Spanish? For 47 days, someone showed up and tried to meet another culture halfway.

We tend to think of our lives as narratives - with arcs, climaxes, and resolutions. But real lives are much more like workshops. There are projects on every surface. Some are done. Most are in various states of becoming. Sawdust on the floor. Paint drying. Instructions lost halfway through.

And that's not a flaw in the design. That *is* the design.

I think we get this idea that we should be master craftsmen of our own lives, that at some point we will finally become competent and streamlined, working on one perfect project at a time until it is complete. But look at any actual craftsman's workshop - any carpenter, any artist, any scientist. Their space is cluttered. They have ten things going at once because their mind has ten curiosities at once. A great mind is not a straight line; it is a branching river delta.

The unfinished reveals something finished things hide: we contain multitudes, and our multitudes don't always agree.

One part of you wants to be a writer. Another part wants to be someone who hikes every weekend. Another part wants to learn to bake sourdough and another part wants to move to another country. You don't have enough time in one life to satisfy them all. So you try. You start. You get a taste. You learn enough to know what it feels like. And then you put it down, not always because you failed, but sometimes because you succeeded just enough. You got what you needed.

Not every meal needs to be eaten until the plate is clean. Sometimes a few bites tells you everything you need to know.

There's a Japanese concept I love called "wabi-sabi" - the beauty of the imperfect, the impermanent, the incomplete. A cracked bowl mended with gold is more beautiful than a perfect bowl, because it has a history. But we rarely apply wabi-sabi to our own ambitions. We want our lives to be perfect bowls, fresh from the kiln. We hide the cracks.

What if we mended our unfinished projects with gold instead? What if we looked at that half-written song and thought, "I learned what it feels like to hear a melody that wasn't there before," rather than "I never finished the song"?

This isn't an argument against finishing things. Finishing is its own kind of magic. There is a profound, quiet pride in pushing something over the finish line when everything in you wants to quit. The world needs people who can finish. Bridges need to be finished. Books need endings. Relationships need commitment.

But finishing should be a choice, not a compulsion. If you finish everything you start, you probably aren't starting enough interesting things.

The fear of leaving things unfinished keeps so many people from starting at all. They won't pick up the watercolors because "What if I'm not good enough to do a whole painting?" They won't try to write because "What if I can't finish a novel?" They have made completeness the entry fee for trying, and the price is too high. So they try nothing.

The museum teaches the opposite: Starting is free. Starting is the point. You are allowed to start a hundred things and finish three. Those three will be better because of the ninety-seven that informed them.

Think about childhood. Children are masters of the unfinished. They build a Lego tower halfway, knock it over, and start building a spaceship. They draw a dinosaur, get bored, and draw a dragon on top of it. They don't finish the game because the *playing* was the purpose, not the winning. Somewhere along the way, we educated that instinct out of them, and ourselves. We taught them that the tower must be tall and stable and photographed for the grandparents.

We need to re-educate ourselves.

I try to practice intentional incompleteness now. I will check a book out of the library knowing I might only read 50 pages. Not because the book is bad, but because those 50 pages might be exactly what I needed, and I don't owe the other 250 pages anything. I will start a course on astronomy not to become an astronomer, but to look at the sky differently for a few weeks. I will plant herbs knowing some will die.

This feels like waste to the efficiency-obsessed part of my brain. That part is always calculating ROI. "If you don't finish, you wasted time." But that part of the brain is terrible at accounting. It doesn't know how to measure wonder on a balance sheet. It can't log the way your hands learned a new rhythm on the guitar strings, even if you never learned a full song. It doesn't count the way your brain was quietly rewired by those 47 days of Spanish.

None of it is wasted. It all becomes compost.

Compost is my other favorite metaphor for this. In a garden, you don't throw away the peelings and leaves that didn't become food. You put them in a pile where they rot beautifully and become soil for whatever comes next. Your unfinished projects are compost. That terrible first draft of a story is compost for the good story you'll write in three years. That awkward, short-lived attempt at meditation is compost for the calmer way you handle stress later.

Nothing is lost if you let it rot correctly.

So tonight, if you have a museum of your own - a drawer of half-finished sketches, a list of abandoned hobbies, a graveyard of good intentions - I hope you can walk through it not with judgment, but with curiosity. Stop at each exhibit. Don't read the plaque that says "Failure." Read the one underneath that says, "Evidence that I tried. Evidence that I was alive and interested in the world."

Ask what each one taught you. Thank it. Leave it there, beautifully unfinished.

Because a life with only finished things in it would be too clean, too empty, too quiet. It would be a showroom, not a home.

I prefer to live in the workshop.

The light is warm. There is sawdust on the floor. There are projects everywhere. And somewhere in the back, on a workbench, is something I am about to start tomorrow, with absolutely no promise that I will ever finish it.

And that, I think, is wonderful.
